prompt: In Horta's table of orders, what is one row?
hint: Observations and variables: one runs across, one runs down.

choices.text: One order
choices.why: Right. Each row is one observation, and here the thing observed is an order.

choices.text: One variable
choices.why: A variable is a column: one property recorded for every order.

choices.text: One customer of the shop
choices.why: A customer who orders four times appears in four rows. This table's rows are orders, which is why 'what is one row?' comes first.

choices.text: One value of the basket column
choices.why: That is a single cell, where one row meets one column.

prompt: Horta's analyst computes the average spend per order and, from another table, the average spend per customer. The two numbers differ. Why?
hint: Ask what one row is in each table.

choices.text: One of the two tables must contain an error
choices.why: Both can be right. They answer different questions because their rows are different things.

choices.text: A customer who orders often is one row in one table and many in the other
choices.why: Right. The rows are different kinds of observation, so each average divides by a different count.

choices.text: Averages of money are never reliable
choices.why: An average of money is a perfectly good summary; the difference here is about what one row is.

choices.text: Customers who order often spend less per order, which drags one average down
choices.why: That might be true and still not explain it: the averages would differ even if every order cost the same, as soon as customers ordered different numbers of times.

prompt: In a table, each row is an ___ and each column is a variable.
hint: The thing that was looked at.

prompt: Which of Horta's columns is categorical?
hint: Which one answers 'which one?' rather than 'how much?'

choices.text: basket, in reais
choices.why: A basket is an amount of money. Arithmetic on it means something, so it is numerical.

choices.text: minutes from order to door
choices.why: A time is a measured quantity, so it is numerical.

choices.text: payment
choices.why: Right. Each order falls into one of pix, card or cash, and the value answers 'which one?'.

choices.text: items in the bag
choices.why: A count of items is a quantity. It is discrete, but it is numerical.

prompt: A frequency table of the neighbourhood column lists 'Barão Geraldo' with 41 orders and 'Barao Geraldo' with 7. What is most likely going on?
hint: Look at what differs between the two names.

choices.text: Two different neighbourhoods with similar names
choices.why: Possible in principle, but a name differing by one accent is the classic symptom of one category typed two ways.

choices.text: One neighbourhood typed two ways, counted as two
choices.why: Right. A computer compares letter by letter, so the true count, 48, is split across two rows of the table.

choices.text: The 7 orders were placed by mistake and should be deleted
choices.why: Nothing says the orders are wrong; only the spelling of their neighbourhood is. Deleting them would lose real orders.

choices.text: The column is numerical and has been read as text
choices.why: A neighbourhood answers 'which one?', so the column is categorical whatever the software thinks.

prompt: Which of these are sensible summaries of the payment column? Choose all that apply.
hint: Every summary of a category starts from a count.

choices.text: How many orders were paid by each method
choices.why: Yes: counting is where every summary of a category starts.

choices.text: The share of orders paid by pix
choices.why: Yes: a share is a count divided by the total.

choices.text: The average payment method
choices.why: There is nothing halfway between pix and card, so an average has nothing to describe.

choices.text: The most common payment method
choices.why: Yes: that is the mode, the one summary of centre a category has.

prompt: What makes Horta's basket column numerical?
hint: Try the test: does arithmetic on it mean anything?

choices.text: It is written in digits
choices.why: So is the postcode, which is not numerical. Digits are a way of writing, not a kind of variable.

choices.text: Its values are amounts, and arithmetic on them means something
choices.why: Right. A difference between two baskets is money, and their total is what the shop took.

choices.text: It has a different value in almost every one of the twelve rows
choices.why: An order number has a different value in every row and is an identifier, not a quantity.

choices.text: It was typed in by the shop's own staff rather than by the customer
choices.why: Who typed it has nothing to do with what kind of variable it is.

prompt: Using the table, how many minutes longer did order H-1048 take than order H-1050?
What is the mean number of items per order across the twelve orders? Give two decimal places.
hint: The twelve counts add up to 75.

prompt: No order had 6.25 items in it, yet the mean is 6.25. What does that say about the mean of a count?
hint: Multiply the mean back by the twelve orders.

choices.text: It is wrong, and should be rounded to 6
choices.why: Rounding throws information away: twelve orders of 6.25 items on average is 75 items, and twelve of 6 is 72.

choices.text: Counts are categorical, so a mean of them is meaningless however it is rounded
choices.why: A count is numerical: the gaps between 1, 2 and 3 items are real, so its mean is meaningful.

choices.text: It is a fair summary that need not be a value any order had
choices.why: Right. A mean describes the whole set; nothing requires any single observation to sit exactly on it.

choices.text: Only continuous variables have a mean
choices.why: Discrete counts have means too, and lesson 2 shows they are used constantly.

prompt: Averaging the twelve postcodes gives 13,044,475.83. What does that number tell Horta?
hint: Ask what the average would mean, in a sentence a manager could act on.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. A postcode names a place; it is not an amount, so its average describes no place and no quantity.

choices.text: The postcode of the typical customer
choices.why: There is no street at 13044-475 that represents the others; averaging codes does not find a middle place.

choices.text: Roughly where the warehouse should be built
choices.why: Postcodes are not coordinates. Neighbouring numbers are not necessarily neighbouring streets.

choices.text: How spread out the deliveries were across the city
choices.why: A mean of codes says nothing about spread, or anything else; the column is categorical.

prompt: Match each column to its kind.
hint: Ask of each one what its average would mean.

pairs.right: yes/no, whose mean is a share

prompt: Of 40 orders, 6 used a voucher. Coded 1 for a voucher and 0 for none, what is the mean of that column?
hint: The column adds up to the number of ones.

prompt: A survey stores satisfaction with delivery as 1 = late, 2 = on time, 3 = early. A report says 'mean delivery: 2.1'. What is the strongest objection?
hint: What happens to the 2.1 if somebody renumbers the codes?

choices.text: It should be reported to more decimal places
choices.why: More decimals would make a meaningless number look more precise, not more meaningful.

choices.text: The mean is fine, but the median would be more precise
choices.why: The trouble is the codes themselves, not which summary is computed from them.

choices.text: The codes are labels, so the 2.1 depends on how they happened to be numbered
choices.why: Right. Number them 1, 3, 2 instead and the 'mean' changes while not one delivery does. A share per category says what the report meant to say.

choices.text: Satisfaction surveys are not data
choices.why: They are data. The fault is treating category codes as amounts.

prompt: Four of the twelve orders were paid by card. What is that as a percentage? Give one decimal place.
In March, 30 orders were paid by card; in April, 45 were. What can you conclude about how popular card payment is?
hint: Thirty out of how many?

choices.text: It grew by half
choices.why: The count grew by half. Whether the habit did depends on how many orders each month had.

choices.text: Nothing yet, without each month's total number of orders
choices.why: Right. Counts compare totals; shares compare habits. 30 of 60 and 45 of 90 are the same share.

choices.text: It fell, because the other payment methods grew even faster
choices.why: Nothing in the question says how the other methods did.

choices.text: It grew by 15 percentage points from one month to the next
choices.why: 15 is a difference in counts, not in percentages; no share has been computed at all.

prompt: A frequency table of 'how did you hear about us' has shares adding up to 134%. What does that tell you?
hint: What would have to happen for the parts to add up to more than the whole?

choices.text: The percentages were rounded
choices.why: Rounding moves a total by a tenth or two, not by 34 points.

choices.text: Some answers were left blank
choices.why: Blank answers would make the shares add up to less, not more, unless they were dropped from the total.

choices.text: Some people were counted in more than one category
choices.why: Right. The question probably allowed several answers, so the categories overlap and the shares no longer describe one population split into parts.

choices.text: The table is numerical and should be averaged
choices.why: 'How did you hear about us' answers 'which one?', so it is categorical.

prompt: In the contingency table, what share of Cambuí's orders were paid by pix? Give a decimal to two places.
hint: Read along Cambuí's row: pix over the row total.

prompt: Put the steps of summarising a new column in the order this lesson recommends.
hint: The formula comes last.
items: Decide what one row of the table is
Ask whether arithmetic on the column means anything
Choose the summaries that kind of variable allows
trap: Computing first is the mistake the lesson warns about: a spreadsheet will average a postcode without complaint.

prompt: Horta adds a column 'customer since', holding the year each customer first ordered, such as 2023. Is it sensible to average it?
hint: Is the gap between 2021 and 2023 something real?

choices.text: No: a year is a label, like a postcode
choices.why: Unlike a postcode, the gap between two years is a real length of time, so arithmetic on years does mean something.

choices.text: Yes, and the average year doubles as the customers' average age
choices.why: The mean year is a date, not an age. To speak of tenure you subtract from the current year, and then you have a quantity.

choices.text: No: averages are only for money and time
choices.why: Averages suit any quantity; the question is whether the column holds one.

choices.text: Yes: differences between years are real lengths of time
choices.why: Right. A mean year of 2022.4 is a meaningful 'typical start', though lesson 2 shows why 'twice the year' would not be.
